item.title: [Logistics 101 #14] The 98% Trap: Why "Almost On Time" Costs You Real Money
item.body:
> A supply chain you can't measure is one you can't defend — this lesson covers the KPIs that matter, the SCOR framework that organizes them, how to price risk before it hits, and why emissions are becoming a logistics metric too.

## Today's Concept

Every warehouse manager will tell you things are "running fine." The job of performance measurement is to replace that sentence with a number.

**Start with KPIs — but the right ones.** The single most useful logistics metric is the **perfect order rate**: the share of orders delivered on time, complete, undamaged, and with correct paperwork. It's brutal because it multiplies:

```
Perfect order rate = on-time % x complete % x damage-free % x correct-docs %
0.98 x 0.98 x 0.98 x 0.98 = 0.922
```

Four "excellent" 98% scores produce a 92% perfect order rate. Eight orders in every hundred go wrong somewhere. That gap between component metrics and end-to-end metrics is where most supply chain complaints live.

Other core measures:

- **Order fulfillment cycle time** — order placed to customer receipt.
- **Cash-to-cash cycle time** — days between paying your supplier and getting paid by your customer: `inventory days + receivable days - payable days`.
- **Inventory turns** and **days of supply** — how hard your working capital is working.
- **Cost to serve** — total logistics cost per order, per unit, or per customer.

**SCOR gives these a home.** The Supply Chain Operations Reference model, maintained by ASCM, is the industry's standard vocabulary. Classic SCOR organizes a supply chain into six process areas — Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return, and Enable — and scores them on five attributes: reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost, and asset management efficiency. The current digital revision (SCOR DS) renames and regroups those processes and folds in environmental and social measures alongside the economic ones. The details shift between versions; the useful idea doesn't. SCOR forces you to say *which attribute* you're optimizing, because you cannot maximize all five. Faster response usually costs more. Lower cost usually means less agility. Pick, then measure.

**Risk management is measurement pointed at the future.** The standard move is a risk register: list what could break, score each item on **likelihood** and **impact**, and multiply to rank. But logistics risk has a twist — the worst events are the low-probability ones, so probability estimates are close to worthless. A more practical pair of questions, popularized by MIT's David Simchi-Levi:

- **Time to Recover (TTR):** if this node goes dark, how long until supply is restored?
- **Time to Survive (TTS):** how long can we keep serving customers on inventory and alternatives?

If TTR exceeds TTS, you have a real exposure, whatever the probability. The fixes are familiar: dual sourcing, safety stock at the right node, qualified backup carriers, postponement (finish the product late, closer to demand), and visibility into tier-2 and tier-3 suppliers — because the plant that shuts down is usually one your buyer has never heard of.

**Sustainability is now a logistics KPI, not a press release.** Transportation and purchased goods sit in **Scope 3** emissions, which for most retailers and manufacturers dwarf their own facilities and fleet. The operational levers are the same ones that cut cost: raise trailer load factor, cut **empty miles**, shift long hauls from truck to intermodal rail, right-size packaging, consolidate LTL shipments into full truckloads. Emissions per ton-mile is the metric; the EPA's SmartWay program is the common US benchmark for carrier performance.

## In Everyday Life

Say you run a Columbus, Ohio distributor selling houseware to a big-box retailer. Your goods move from a supplier in Vietnam, through the Port of Long Beach, by rail to Chicago, then by truck to your DC.

Your internal dashboard looks great: 97% on-time from the DC, 99% pick accuracy. Then your retail customer's scorecard arrives. Large chains run **OTIF (on-time, in-full)** programs and charge suppliers for misses — Walmart's has assessed fees of roughly 3% of the value of noncompliant goods. On $8 million of annual shipments to that account, a 10% miss rate is about $24,000 in fines, plus expedited freight to chase the shortfalls, plus a worse position in next year's negotiation.

Then the port slows down for three weeks. You dig into your risk register and find the honest numbers: TTR for that ocean lane is 5 weeks; your TTS on current inventory is 3 weeks. Two weeks exposed. The options each carry a price you can actually compute — air freight a partial order at maybe $4–6 per kilogram versus roughly $0.30 by ocean, hold four extra weeks of safety stock at a carrying cost of 20–25% of inventory value per year, or qualify a second supplier at a few months of engineering time.

None of those choices is obvious. But once you've written down the perfect order rate, the fine schedule, TTR versus TTS, and the carrying cost, you're making a business decision instead of a guess.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Component metrics lie; end-to-end metrics like perfect order rate and cash-to-cash tell the truth, because errors multiply rather than average.
2. SCOR provides shared language and forces the trade-off — reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost, and assets cannot all be maximized at once.
3. Manage risk by comparing time-to-recover with time-to-survive rather than guessing probabilities, and treat emissions per ton-mile as a real KPI alongside cost.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** A shipper hits 99% on-time, 98% complete, 99% damage-free, and 100% correct documentation. What is the perfect order rate?
  A) 99.0%  B) 98.0%  C) about 96.0%  D) 100%

**2. (O/X)** A disruption with very low probability can safely be ignored in a risk register.

**3.** Cash-to-cash cycle time is calculated as:
  A) inventory days + receivable days − payable days
  B) receivable days + payable days − inventory days
  C) order cycle time + transit time
  D) revenue ÷ average inventory

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Perfect Order Rate** — Share of orders delivered on time, complete, undamaged, and correctly documented; the four rates multiply.
- **SCOR** — The Supply Chain Operations Reference model, an ASCM-maintained standard for describing supply chain processes and scoring their performance.
- **Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time** — Days of working capital tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.
- **TTR / TTS** — Time to Recover from a disrupted node versus Time to Survive on existing inventory; exposure exists when TTR is longer than TTS.
- **Scope 3 Emissions** — Indirect emissions from purchased goods and outsourced transportation, typically the largest share of a shipper's carbon footprint.

---

*Answers: 1 — C. 0.99 x 0.98 x 0.99 x 1.00 = 0.960, about 96%; four strong scores still leave four bad orders per hundred. 2 — X. Rank by impact as well as likelihood; low-probability, high-impact events are exactly the ones that require a survival plan, since probability estimates for rare events are unreliable. 3 — A. Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days; paying suppliers later and collecting sooner shortens the cycle.*
